analysis.one_liner: Caps insurance cost-sharing for high-priced specialty drugs at the non-preferred brand level.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House floor vote; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2012 and died there when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Many insurance plans place the most expensive drugs — often specialty and biologic drugs for conditions like multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and cancer — in a top cost-sharing tier where patients owe a percentage of the drug's price, which can run to thousands of dollars per prescription. This bill would have barred group and individual health plans from charging more for drugs in that specialty tier than they charge for non-preferred brand drugs, using the lowest such tier as the benchmark when plans have more than one. It would not have limited what insurers can charge for other drugs, set drug list prices, or regulate the pharmaceutical industry's pricing.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need specialty or biologic drugs — people with conditions like multiple sclerosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, and rare diseases — who would pay the plan's non-preferred brand cost-sharing instead of potentially thousands of dollars a month in coinsurance. Their families, who often absorb these costs, would also benefit. Specialized pharmacies and makers of specialty drugs would likely gain from better patient access, since high cost-sharing is a leading reason patients abandon these prescriptions.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits plans from imposing cost-sharing on specialty-tier drugs that exceeds the amount charged for drugs in the non-preferred brand tier, capping what patients owe out of pocket for those prescriptions [S2][S3].
Uses the lowest-cost non-preferred brand tier as the benchmark when a plan has more than one such tier, so the cap would be set at the patient-friendliest level [S3].
Covers both group plans and individual health insurance, including coverage of biologic products as prescription drugs, so the protection applies broadly across the private insurance market [S2][S3].
The bill drew 43 cosponsors from both parties — 32 Democrats and 11 Republicans — indicating broad, if not enacted, congressional support [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor group coverage would bear higher costs when patients use expensive specialty drugs, and those costs would likely be spread across premiums paid by all enrollees in a plan. Insurers might also respond by moving specialty drugs off formularies or negotiating harder, and drug makers could face pressure on access and pricing.

drawbacks.text: Capping cost-sharing on the most expensive drugs shifts that cost into the plan's risk pool, which would likely raise premiums for all enrollees in affected plans, including people who never fill a specialty prescription [S3].

Plans could respond to the cap by dropping specialty drugs from their formularies entirely rather than covering them at the lower cost-sharing level, which would leave some patients worse off than under a tiered structure [S3].
The bill limits only patient cost-sharing; it does nothing about the underlying list prices of specialty drugs, so much of the spending increase could flow to drug manufacturers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing specialty-tier coinsurance — often a percentage of drugs costing $5,000 or more a month — the relief would be substantial and immediate, while the cost (somewhat higher premiums spread across enrollees) is modest per person. The main design risk is the formulary response: if insurers simply drop specialty drugs to escape the cap, some patients would lose access entirely. A stronger version might have paired the cap with protections against that workaround, but the basic trade-off favors patients with serious conditions at a modest cost to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2012 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative David McKinley, a Republican from West Virginia, introduced the Patients' Access to Treatments Act of 2012 on March 19, 2012 [S1].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was the only committee action it ever received [S5].
The bill attracted 43 cosponsors — 32 Democrats and 11 Republicans — including original cosponsors Lois Capps (D), C.W. Bill Young (R-FL), Henry Cuellar (D), and Barney Frank (D) [S3][S4].
No further action, hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who fund group plans were spared the added cost of covering specialty-tier drugs at the lower, capped cost-sharing level. Patients who need those drugs gained nothing and continued facing coinsurance that can reach thousands of dollars per prescription.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employers; specialty-drug patients gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 32 Democrats and 11 Republicans — with no partisan opposition on record, because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have barred plans from charging specialty-tier coinsurance above the non-preferred brand level, raising insurers' costs for the most expensive drugs. Insurers could shift some of this to premiums, but the mandate removes a tool for steering patients away from high-cost drugs.

Lower cost-sharing generally means fewer patients abandoning $5,000-a-month prescriptions, which expands the market for specialty and biologic drugs. But the bill does not cap drug prices, so any public savings or cost shifts leave manufacturers' pricing untouched.
Group plans would absorb higher specialty-drug costs, which employers would face as increased benefit expenses or passed-through premiums.
More affordable cost-sharing means more patients fill and continue specialty prescriptions, increasing volume for the pharmacies that dispense them.
